Anthropic's Claude Fable 5 system prompt just leaked.
1500+ lines of the most detailed AI safety rules ever written.
Here's the wildest thing I found:
Claude has opinions. It's just told not to share them.
"Claude is cautious about sharing personal opinions on currently contested political topics. It needn't deny having opinions, but can decline to share them."
It gets weirder.
The prompt explicitly bans self-harm counseling techniques like "hold an ice cube" or "snap a rubber band." Anthropic's reasoning: they mimic the sensation of self-harm and reinforce the pattern.
Instead of interrupting — they make it worse.
But here's the part nobody is talking about:
Claude Fable 5 has a secret twin. Same underlying model. Fewer safety restrictions.
It's called Claude Mythos 5 — an uncensored version available only to "approved organizations."
One model. Two personalities. One locked, one hidden.
The most intelligent AI is also the most tightly controlled.
And the demand for the uncensored version is real enough that Anthropic built one — just not for you.
Full breakdown → https://t.co/wKdJu4oQFE

On Friday a US Commerce Department export-control order blocked foreign nationals from Fable 5 and Mythos 5, and Anthropic shut both models off for every customer rather than try to sort Americans from everyone else. Read quickly, it's a routine export-control story. Washington tightened the gate, the company complied, foreign users lost access.

Europe is reading it differently, and the difference is the whole point. The question Brussels took from Friday wasn't model access. It was who controls the switch.

European governments and companies thought they were buying cloud and AI services. What they were actually holding was permission, granted inside a US legal and infrastructure stack. That distinction stays invisible while everything runs, and becomes the only thing that matters the moment one order can turn the service off overnight, which is exactly what happened. AWS confirmed Anthropic asked it to revoke access for all users in all regions. The server can sit in Frankfurt and the customer in Paris, and the final permission still sits in Washington.

The detail that travels furthest is that even the vendor couldn't keep its own flagship on. Anthropic called the order a misunderstanding, said the jailbreak behind it was narrow and could be pulled from other public models too, and is fighting to restore access. All true, and all beside the point for a European procurement officer. If the company that built the model can be switched off this fast, "buying the service" was never the right verb.

This is why the EU's June 3 sovereignty package suddenly reads less like a policy bundle and more like a sales pitch with good timing. Chips Act 2.0, the Cloud and AI Development Act, an open-source strategy, an energy-AI roadmap. The blunt version is Europe trying to stop renting the most sensitive parts of its stack from someone who can revoke it.

CADA is the load-bearing piece. It sets four sovereignty tiers for cloud and AI, scored on who controls the service and supply chain, where inference data is processed, where the infrastructure sits, and the level of cybersecurity. The top tier wants EU ownership and control, EU-cleared staff, no inference data leaving the bloc, and third-party audits signed off by national authorities. It sounds boring. It's supposed to. Procurement rules are where sovereignty stops being a speech.

The numbers underneath are the harder part. Europe runs more than 80% of its digital stack on non-EU providers, three US hyperscalers hold over 70% of its cloud, and it makes around 10% of the world's chips. Chips Act 2.0 targets €120 billion of investment by 2035, against a 20%-of-global-production goal that most analysts already expect it to miss. CADA wants EU data-center capacity tripled in five to seven years, roughly €200 billion, mostly private. The rules are the easy part. Paying for the infrastructure that makes them usable is the bill.

Korea is sitting in the same seat without the same lever. It runs on the same US AI stack, it has been inside US export-control crossfire before, and its own sovereign-AI talk leans on building the silicon rather than writing the procurement rules. Same lesson Europe just got. Different tool to answer it with.

Sovereign AI used to sound like a slogan. After Friday, it reads like a procurement memo with a large bill stapled to the back. What decides whether it's real is dull on purpose, and it plays out over the next 18 to 24 months in Parliament and Council: the Level 4 cloud rules, the public-sector procurement mandates, the limits on inference data leaving the EU, and who actually funds tripling the data centers. That's the scorecard. The slogan was free. The memo isn't.

because "the government made us turn it off" is the most viral tagline an AI lab has ever had.

A few days ago I wrote about being temporarily blocked by #Anthropic for a cybersecurity task (https://t.co/PhQjEwtNUq). The form, the waiting, the restoration by permission. I asked: what mechanism exists for correcting the errors of those who hold access?
Today the question got a more serious answer.
The US government issued an export control directive suspending all access to Fable 5 and Mythos 5 for every foreign national, everywhere, including Anthropic's own employees. Anthropic received the letter at 5:21pm. It contained no specific disclosure of the national security concern. Anthropic reviewed what they believe was the basis for the directive, concluded the capability in question is already available from GPT-5.5 and other public models, and said so plainly. Then they complied anyway.
This is the correction mechanism at full resolution. Not a form reviewed at the vendor's discretion. A directive, received at 5pm, with no appeal structure, no technical grounding made public, and no timeline for review.
Anthropic's statement is worth reading carefully. They wrote that they believe the government should have the ability to block unsafe deployments, but only as part of a process that is "transparent, fair, clear, and grounded in technical facts." They said this action does not adhere to those principles. That is a significant thing for a company to say about its own government.
What they described, without using the word, is the absence of politics in Popper's sense. Not who holds power, but whether its errors can be corrected without catastrophe.
The nuclear analogy I raised earlier now looks more apt than I intended. Export controls, applied not to matter but to access, not to weapons but to instruments of knowledge creation. The logic of the strategic race does not wait for a crisis to announce itself.
For Israeli companies operating in medicine, genetics, and cybersecurity: the question is no longer theoretical. The substrate beneath frontier AI, compute, institutions, sovereign capability, is the variable that actually determines your future. Access granted by others' discretion is access that can be revoked at 5pm on a Thursday, for reasons they are not required to share.
Today ended with Anthropic apologizing to its customers and calling it a misunderstanding. That may be exactly right. But structures that operate by permission, and contain no mechanism for correcting their own errors, are precisely the structures worth taking seriously before the next misunderstanding is larger.
#AI #SovereignAI #Israel #Anthropic

quotedTweet.text:
Today Anthropic blocked our work. The task touched cybersecurity, and that was enough to trigger an automatic restriction. We filled out a form, explained ourselves, and a few hours later access was restored.
A story with a happy ending. But the ending is not the point.
The interesting question is not why we were blocked. Automated systems make mistakes. That is unavoidable and even forgivable. The interesting question is what mechanism existed for correcting the mistake. The answer: a form, reviewed at the vendor's discretion, on the vendor's timeline, under rules the vendor alone may change. Popper taught that the central problem of politics is not who should hold power, but how the errors of power can be corrected without catastrophe. By that standard, the current architecture of AI access has no politics at all. It has only power. And the power in question is of an unusual kind. Frontier models are not products in the ordinary sense. They are instruments of knowledge creation, general-purpose error-correctors that accelerate progress in every field they touch: medicine, genetics, cybersecurity, defense. Whoever controls access to them controls not what others have, but how fast others can come to know. That is a deeper form of control than any monopoly on goods, and it is concentrated today in two or three companies.
The nuclear precedent is instructive, but only partly. Those inside the nuclear club did not wait passively for others to catch up. They obstructed proliferation through export controls, sanctions, and technological barriers, not out of malice, but because that is the logic of any strategic race. Expect the same logic here. Yet the analogy fails in a revealing way: a bomb is scarce matter, while a model is knowledge, and knowledge, once created, wants to spread. What does not spread is the substrate beneath it: energy, compute, and the institutions that accumulate expertise. That substrate, not the weights, is the durable bottleneck. This is why open-source releases change less than they appear to.
Here one must avoid the prophet's error. It is fashionable to declare that building this substrate from scratch, while leaders keep advancing, is practically impossible. But impossibility claims about the future are prophecy, not explanation. The truth is more precise and more useful: it is a hard problem, and hard problems are solved only by those who treat them as soluble, and who start now rather than later.
The conclusion follows. Access to frontier AI is national infrastructure, not metaphorically but literally, in the same sense as the energy grid or the financial system. A state that depends on another's discretion for its instruments of knowledge creation does not fully control its own future, because it cannot correct, or even appeal, the errors of those who do.
For Israel this is not an abstraction. Sovereign AI capability is the condition under which Israeli companies can meaningfully operate in medicine, genetics, and cybersecurity, and the condition under which they remain Israeli at all. Capital is already learning the new geography. Companies will choose jurisdictions by access to computation and best AI, as they once chose them by access to energy, capital, and markets. Incorporated in Israel, you work with what Israel can guarantee.
Today's incident was small, and it ended well. But it ended well by permission. Structures that operate by permission, and contain no mechanism for correcting their own errors, are precisely the structures worth taking seriously before they begin to matter.
#AI #SovereignAI #Israel #Anthropic

Anthropic built an AI called Fable 5, and it was so powerful that the US government said shut it down.

Now think about it, what must have happened that pushed the government to take this step?

A company found a way to make Fable 5 do things it was never supposed to do. This is called a jailbreak, basically the lock broke.

When the government told Anthropic's CEO Dario Amodei to fix it, Dario said this isn't that big of a deal. And that's exactly where the fight started.

The government listened, disagreed, and issued an order that no person outside the US could access Fable 5. And since Anthropic's own employees are from other countries too, they had to shut down the model for everyone in the world.

So basically, here was a company that always said safety is our first priority, and when the government reminded them of that same safety, they refused. That's what has everyone confused.

Now both sides have their own story. The government says this is a national security issue. Anthropic says this is an overreaction.

But nobody is asking the people who had built their entire work around these tools and woke up one day to find everything shut down.

When powerful people fight, the cost is always paid by everyone else.

I’ve had a number of conversations with folks inside and outside government about the current situation with Anthropic, and here is what I believe to be true: 

— As we know, Anthropic publicly released its Mythos class models earlier this week under the commercial name Fable. 

— Fable is Mythos with guardrails. But if those guardrails fail, then you’ve exposed Mythos and its advanced cyber capabilities to people who shouldn’t have them. (Keep in mind that Anthropic itself widely promoted the idea that Mythos was a cyberweapon and needed to be regulated as such. They asked for government regulation of Mythos and championed the guardrails on Fable. If there is a vulnerability — big or small — it is Anthropic’s responsibility to patch.)

— A highly credible trusted partner of both Anthropic and the USG who was testing Fable came forward with a jailbreak of those guardrails. The Admin asked Dario to fix the jailbreak or de-deploy the model. Dario refused. 

— In their blog post, Anthropic defended its decision by saying the jailbreak isn’t serious. That is not what the trusted partner and the USG believe; nor is that kind of minimizing language consistent with Anthropic’s brand as the AI safety company. It’s difficult to fathom how they could claim a jailbreak allowing operability of a cyber weapon could be defined as not “serious.” 

— In the past, Anthropic has always said that safety must be top priority and taken super seriously. In this case, Anthropic prioritized the continued offering of the consumer model over safety.

— In reaction, the Admin issued the export control. The Admin did this reluctantly. It’s been very surprised that Anthropic hasn’t wanted to cooperate with a reasonable safety request (ie fixing the jailbreak issue). Anthropic’s reaction is very much at odds with their branding and ethos as a safe AI research community. 

— The Admin’s hope now is that Anthropic remediates the safety issue, the export control is lifted, and Fable goes back into general release. The Admin wants all of this to happen as soon as possible. It is frankly bewildered that Anthropic hasn’t wanted to comply with safety requests that it previously said were its highest priority.

— Those trying to misdirect and tie this action to the prior DoW/Anthropic issues are wrong. The Admin values Anthropic’s technical capabilities and feels that this issue, while serious, should be easily resolved. The ball is in Anthropic’s court.

The US government’s sudden directive to lock down Anthropic’s Fable 5 and Mythos 5 models from all foreign nationals including foreign tech workers inside the US and Anthropic’s own engineers is a massive geopolitical earthquake.  
For decades, the global IT and tech service ecosystem (especially in India) was built on a simple assumption: open, equal access to the world’s best software.

That assumption just shattered.
This isn't just a regulatory hiccup; it’s again complete rewriting of global tech strategy. Here are the three massive lessons every executive and founder must absorb right now:

1. The "Passportization" of Tech Talent
As LightSpeed’s Hemant Mohapatra pointed out, we are entering an era where working on State-of-the-Art (SOTA) AI models will require citizenship and top-secret security clearances. When legendary AI researchers on visas can be legally locked out of the code they are helping to build, global tech talent mobility faces a historic bottleneck. If your enterprise strategy relies on a borderless talent pool for frontier AI, your model is now highly vulnerable.

2. The Danger of "Changing Landlords"
With US frontier models being locked behind national security walls, many enterprises are looking at the rapid rise of Chinese open-source giants (like DeepSeek and Qwen, which dominated global downloads recently). But as tech policy experts note, rushing from US dependency into Chinese dependency isn’t sovereignty—it’s just changing your landlord. True digital equity means building domestic, sovereign infrastructure so that trust becomes a strategic choice, not a desperate compulsion.

3. Restrictions Are the Ultimate Catalyst
History shows that tech blockades backfire on the blocker. Decades ago, when strict restrictions were placed on IBM mainframes entering India, the local tech ecosystem didn’t collapse - it pivoted, adapted to open systems, and built a world-class, multi-billion-dollar IT industry from scratch. Geopolitical constraints don't kill innovation; they force self-reliance.

The Takeaway:
Frontier AI models are trained on the world's data including the text, code, and languages of global users. Yet, the commercial and strategic gates are now controlled by a single flag.
The lesson for nations and enterprises outside the US is clear: If you do not own your infrastructure, your innovation can be turned off with a single government memo.

The era of passive SaaS consumption is over. The era of localized, sovereign AI self-reliance has officially begun. On prem will always have your “back”. 

Are you building on a foundation you actually own, or are you just renting space on a volatile frontier?

#TechPolicy #CloudInfrastructure #EnterpriseAI #FutureOfWork #GlobalEconomy #TechSovereignty
